"His Majesty the King of Denmark, Duke of Holstein and Lauenbourg, having made known by the declaration of the 7th of Sept. in reply to the petition addressed to the Diet by the states of Holstein, on the 3d of August that there never was any intention of attacking the independence of the Duchy of Holstein, nor of modifying arbitrarily either the constitution or the other institutions which the usage and laws of the country have consecrated ; his .Majesty having, besides, given the assurance that ihe efforts to regulate the order of the succession of that Duchy were not intended to affect the legitimate l ights of the agnates, and, in short, t he intention to maintain enti'e the constitutional right of petition by t fie states having been openly acknowledged by his Majesty the High Diet is confident that in coming to a definitive resolution on t fie subject, of which the Liter patent of the 8th of July makes mention his Majesty will respect the rights of all, and particularly the rights of the Confederation, the legitimate rights of the agnates, and those of the legal representatives of the country. Wlule reserving to itself, as organ of the Confederation, ihe right of giving effect, shouid the case arise, to its constitutional competence, the Diet deems that it cannot receive in the states of Holstein the legal representatives of that federal state ; that their mission should be limited to the defence of their constitutional rights; and that the complaint of these states on the subject of

changes to be made in an illegal manner in their constitution is without foundation. On the other hand, the Diet deems that the order transmitted by his Majesty to the royal commissioners at these states, not to receive petitions or reclamations relating to t fie question of the succession, does not, strictly speaking, accord with the literal sense of the law of tfie 28th of May, 1831. " Secondly þÿ The Diet is gratified in rendering justice <o the patriotic sentiments that have been manifested on this occasion in Germany, hut it deplores the hostile charges and expressions of animosity that have been given vent to. It hopes and trusts that the confederated governments will endcavnnr to put a stop to this agitation and excitement: and it has no doubt hut that his Majesty t fie King of Denmark will fully reciprocate that feeling.

5 l> A / /V. The Protest of Don Enrique (younger brother of the successful candidate for the hand of the young Queen! against the Montpensier match is too important not to be given at length. It is dated Ghent, Sept. 0. and copies of it have been placed in the hands of the Presidents of both Houses of Congress, and a third copy, it is said, tins been sent to the Queen Don Enrique is also said to have written to his brother Don Francisco, to complain ofhis breach of faith in reference to the Montpensier match, to which, when himself a candidate for the hand of Isabella, he had always refused to consent.

PROTEST Ob DON ENRIQUE. " The Cortes will soon be assembled, and to that body must a persecuted Prince elevate his voice from his place of exile. To addtess the Government would certainly be useless þÿ to appeal to the nation might be considered dangerous ; the Cortes alone will know how to reconcile what is due to the tranquility of the country with what is due to its Princes and to the future destiny of the royal family. demote from the Court and all ambitious views, I lived exclusively devoted to the duties ol mv profession as a sailor, when with the lloyal permission, 1 repaired, tow. ards the end of the year 1645, to visit my revered father at Madrid. In his paternal a flection, and guided more or less by what he knew or imagined of the Queen's wishes, he thought that I was inn position to take some initiative in lite important question of her marriage; for myself, taking into consideratioo t he public opinion as unanimously manifested by the press of all parties, I thought 1 could not take such a step w ithout declaring in writing, and that in the most solemn manner, the political principles which ought to he observed in a matter so important for the security of the Constitutional throne and the independence of the Spanish nation. My father undertook to present in my name to her Majesty the expressions of my sentiments. The circumstances which occurred at the Koyal palace on this occasion obliged me to publish my manifesto of the 31st Oecemhar, which could not be understood as

the motive of its publication remained unknown. « Prom that moment commenced for me a period of persecution, which has hardly beheld a day pass without some fresh injury being levelled at me. « I will not descend to enumerate the various vexations which I suffered, i he most public and notorious will sulliee to show whether or not they ought from the past to adopt some measure which, for the future, may prevent a prince, or any other Spaniard, from being the victim of the arbitrary will of their Ministers. . Having obliged me to quit Madrid immediately, 1 was received and treated by the authorities of Galicia, in a way which taught me to know the other trials to which the Ministers had resolved to subject me. The regard of my countrymen, which, however, they were not allowed to show me, compensated nevertheless for the vexations I endured, uid never did I enjoy greater peace ol mind, aud moie complete tranquility, than

STa V 'Ji D1Z ATI 3 during the first period of my persecution Nor did I dream of obtaining a position which would have forced mv persecutors to respect me) on the contrary, 1 longed, lioin the bottom of mv heart, ns the greatest bap piness for the Queen and for the nation, that the choice of her Majesty should fall on my beloved brother, as more worthy to occupy so distinguished arid high a position þÿ a sentiment which 1 have ever manifested with loyalty whenever the opportunity lor so doing was afforded me. " After this sincere proof of self denial given bv me at that time, and living as I was in tranquility and exile, 1 could not at that tune understand the motives of the iresh persecution which assailed me, wheu, being in Ferrol, I received the order to present myseil without a moment's ioss ol time at Coiunna, beloie the Captain General of Galicia. who communicated to me the order which 1 e .close, to the effect that 1 should quit the kingdom in forty two hours, in spite of any impediment, I might oppose to the contrary, even that of illness þÿ a circumstance mentioned in the Government order, which was communicated to me on my embarking, but w Inch 1 have not in my possession. (Jut of respect for lite Queen and love ol peace, 1 consented to this indignity, and writing to her Majesty in fitting terms, 1 emhaiked for Bayopue, without even receiving the bottoms due to my rank on leaving the shores of my country, and the object of the cruel prejudices excited against me in the mind of the com-

mandant of the vessel which conveyed me, and who was required to give a receipt for my person In as far as the action and power ol the Ministers could reach me in a foreign land. I expeiienccd the effects of iheir rage. 1 could not comprehend the tine motive and object which they had in view until 1 arrived in l'aiis, where 1 was so kindly received by my august uncle, the King of the French, when I petceived cleat ly that it was not the act of having one day aspired to the hand of Iter Majesty thai was to be punished in me, but the not continuing to do so, accompanying my desire with submission loa certain influence, and combining it with a certain condition. 1 never intended to mention this, but to the National Assembly 1 owe the whole truth, and I will not fail in this duty any more than 1 did at Faris in those which bind me towards my country and my family- « 1 quickly left that capital lor this peaceful kingdom, where 1 have lived retiredly and tranquil, although calumniated, calmly awaiting the solution of the quesiion which was to bear so much inlluence on my future destiny. Proposals Irom, in my eyes, the most respectable quarter, have been made to me to return to Spain. Had 1 consulted my own personal interest I should have accepted them: but attentive only to my dignity and to t lie severe principles which I have laid down for my guidance, I rejected them, declaring that 1 have a right to require, and that 1 must sooner or later obtain, reparation as complete and honourable as the injustice

of my ejection from the kingdom of Spain was great. " The silence which followed these communications might naturally have been expected to be the forerunner of some catastrophe, and such, indeed, it has proved þÿ the marriage of her Majesty the Qoecn with my beloved brother, and that of the Infanta w ith the Duke of Montpcusier, agreed upon at the

same time, although not puhlisl ebin the s; n e form, solemnly announced to Spam The first accomplishes mv wishes so often manifested, and the second discovers to Spain and the whole of Europe that which 1 was given to understand during mv stiort residence in Paris. Of the use whie.lt Spain and Europe may make of (his discovery 1 have nothing to say, nor does it belong to me to examine whether a clause inserted in the Constitution in the year 1815 opposes litis union. What belongs to me by right, and that which I shall do, influenced less by family views and interests than by the desire to avoid 1 he possibility of difficult questions, and perhaps even wars of succession, which have been so fatal to Spain, is to protest against all eventual right to the Crown which may tie granted to lite children of the Duke of Montpensier, if he should ever be united to the infanta. " The renunciation which the family of Ot leans made by the treaty of Uliecht would annul beforehand any right of this kind wh eh might be declared or supposed, and my family being the one most injured, I protest before the Cortes against any piejudiee which may arise. ' Thus, the present document, which 1 respectfully address to the Senate, will serve at the same time to enable the Cortes to adopt the necessary measures that for the future, and bv their orders, the anlecedt nt rights of all and such of the individuals of the royal family should tie respected as the basis of the tranquility and independence of the
nation, which, wheresoever I may he, is, and will remain, the idol of my heart, as it is of every good Spaniard, no matter what may be his party. " E.MtlQt'E l)e BotltDON. " Ghent, Sept. 9, 1640."

Taylor arrived before Monterey, with a force of about (5000 men, and alter reconnoitering the city at about ioOO or 1(500 yards from the Calhedia! fort, during which he was fired upon from its batteries, Ins force was encamped at the Walnut Springs, 3 miles shot l of the city. This was the nearest position at which the army could obtain a supply of w ater, and be beyond the reach of the enemy's batteries. The remainder of the 10th was occupied by the engineers in making reconnoisances of the city, l atteries and commanding heights On the 20th Gen. Worth was ordered with his division to move by a circuitous route to the light, to gain the Saltill road beyond the west of the tofrn and to storm the heights above the Bishop's I'alace, which vital point the enemy appears to have strangely neglected. Circumstances caused Ins halt on the night of the 20.h, short of the intended position On the morning of the 2 1st he continued his route, and after an encounter with a large body of the enemy's cavalry arid infantry, supported by artillery from the heights, he repulsed them with loss, and finally encamped, covering the passage of the Saltillo road. It was here discovered, that besides the lort at the Bishop's Palace and the occupation of the heights above it, two forts, on commanding eminences, on the opposite side oi the San Juan, had been fortified and occupied. These two latter heights were then

stormed and carried þÿ the guns of the last fort carried being immediately turned with a plunging fire upon the Bishop's Palace. On this same morning (the 21st) the 1st Division of regular troops, under Gen. Twiggs, and the Volunteer Division under Gen. Butler, were ordered under arms to make a diversion to the left of the town, in favor of the important operations of Gen. Worth. The 10 inch mortar and two 24 pounder howitzers, had been put in battery the night of the 20th, in a ravine 1400 "yards distant from the Cathedral fort or Citadel, and were supported by the 4th Regiment of Infantry. At 8 a m. on the 21st the order was given for this battery to open upon the citadel and town, and immediately after the 1st division, with the 3rd and 4th infantry in advance, under Col. Garland, weic ordered to reconnoitre and skirmish with the enemy on the exlreme left of the city, and should prospect of success offer, to carry the most advanced batterv. þÿ This attack was directed by Major Mansfield, Engineer, Capt. Williams, Topographical Engineer, and Major Kinney, Q. M. to the Texas Division. A heavy fire from the fust battery was immediately opened upon the advance, but the troops soon tinned it, entering and engaging with the enemy in the streets of the city having passed through an incessant cross fire from the Citadel and the first and second butteries, and from the infan-

The 1st Division was followed and supported by the Mississippi and Tennessee and 1st Ohio Regiments, the 2 lot trier regiments being the hist to scale and occupy the lort. The success of the day here slopped. The Mississippi, Tennessee and Ohio regiments, though warmly engaged in the streets of the city lor some time after the capture of the 1st battery and us adjoining defences, were unable, from exhaustion and the loss they bad suffered, to gain more advantage. A heavy shower of rain also came up to cause a suspension of hostilities befote the close of the day. The 3d, 4th and 1st Infantry and the Baltimore Battalion, remained as the gutiison of the captuied position, under Gol. Gat laud, assisted by Gapt Ridgely's battery. Blanchard perfoimcd efficient and gallant service as part ol Cnptajn Vinton's command. On the evening ol the 22d, (Jul Garland and bis command were relieved as the garrison of the captuied lorts by Gen. Quitman with the Mississippi and Tennessee Regiments, and five companies of the Kentucky Regiment. Early on the morning of the 23d, General Quitman, front his position, discovered that the second and third torts and defences east of the city had been entirely abandoned by the enemy, who apprehended another assault on the night of the 22nd had retired from till his defences to the main plaza and its immediate vicinity. A command of two companies of Mississippi and two of Tennessee troops were then thrown into the streets to reconnoitre, and soon became holly engaged with the enemy, these wete soon supported by Gol. Wood's regiment of Texas Rangers, dismounted, by Bragg's Light Battery and the 3rd Infantry ; the enemy's fire was constant and uninterrupted ftom the streets, house tops, barricades, &o. &c in the vicinity

of the plaza. The Trent arrived from Jamaica this morning at 7 o'clock, the news she brings is distressing and momentous in the extreme as will be admitted by perusing the extracts which we have made from our files. Full particulars of an awful hurricane which occurred at the Havana on the JOth and 11th ult. ate among the incidents. By the same steamer which left Carthagena On the 28th ult we learn that considerable excitement prevailed at that place, and at Santa Martha, in consequence of the reported departure of General Florres ex President of the Republic of Equador from Old Spain, with a body of 5000 men 500 of whom were said to be English, with hostile intentions towards that country. At Santa Martha orders had been issued to place the forts in a state of defence, and to have the troops and the militia force ready for service,

On the arri val of the boats from Demerara and Vera Cruz at St Thomas, the goods and passengers brought by them will be transferred to larger Steamers, which will proceed th'-nee to New York calling at Bermuda. They expect to reach New York in time to meet the British and North American Steam Boa! for Boston, Halifax and Liverpool. On the arrival of the English Mail by the Cnriard Steamers at New York, the Company's Steamers will return to St. Thomas via Ber-

muda. The establishment of such a direct line of communication with the Windward Islands n (id Demerara would be of much importance to our commercial community and others, for by the present circuitous route of the Itoyal Mail Steamers, letters or passengers do not reach Barbadoes until one month from the date of leaving Bermuda. It would fotm a link in the chain of communication between the North American provinces, Bermuda and the West Indies, which we have long desired to see effected. Snakes in Australia. þÿ A friend, who had been out shooting for some hours, coming home tired, without thought reliction was or on the point of throwing himself on a stretcher to re?!, when tie was suddenly pul.ed hack hy a bystander, who find observed a tremendous blown snake coih-d up on the opossum cloak He w a horrified, but providentially -saved 'I'ltc snake, of course, was goon dispatched. Another friend, on a ciuise, pul his saddle down fora pillow at night as usual, and on lifting up the saddle flips ihe next morning, lie observed a beastly dt af adder lying fl it down, lie noon dropped tfie saddle, and killed the snake V\ bile giving <ur hotscs water one day, my cousin saw a black snake, half in ami half out of the water ; he shot it and put it upon an ant full to wauh the ants at work. While so er gaged, ns mate uawe at us, jtassing ovei my lustcp, iu

a state of great excitement 5 it was also shot. Ongoing over the Main Kange, a deaf adder was observed, creeping on a poor quail which crouched on the ground, fascinated ; we allowed the poor bird to fall a victim ; and then struck at the adder. The blow did not take þÿeffect, and the reptile sprang three feet at my triend, who escaped unhurt; the adder was subsequently killed. Again, being one day encamped on the Main Kange, for the purpose of cutting bark w ith my bruther and a friend. I had to go down to a little waterhole to fill the quart pots for tea ; while stooping down to iny task, an enormous black snake slid down the bank, quacking and his sing ; before I could recover from my fright, he had passed over my arm, and up the op posite bank. ) was too much terrified to shoot at him, though 1 had my gun at my side. Two more instances will suffice þÿ a little child, the daughter of a friend of mine, playing on the verandah, was on the point of picking up what site thought a varnished piece of woi d þÿ so flat and straight was it extended when her father called her back. þÿ The snake (for such the piece of wood turned out to be) basking in the sun, proved to be a large diamond snake about nine feet long. þÿ Again, l was sitting with my sister, after the children were pul to bed, and having heaid that a snake had been seen in the house during the day, we were frightened. Kains irr Australia. þÿ The thunder-storms in Australia are tremendous, sudden, and frequent; in an hour the whole surface is covered with water, and little courses roll down the hills in torrents. 1 have seen cattle tracks, a little worn below the surface, carrying off the water; they become dry and crack ; the next rain converts the crack into a fissure, which gradually widens and extends itself till it becomes a large gulley. þÿ On old used dray-roads tire quantity of little streams is surprising, caused in a similar way. 1 have seen a thrice reflected rainbow during one of these storms. 1 have seen whole forests denuded of every leaf, and ns hare as a wood in the winter season in England. I have seen the grass beaten down so that not a blade could be seen erect, and the earth go full of little marks that 1 fancied a flock of sheep had been over it. This was caused bv a hailstorm iu the month of September þÿ 1 have known a shepherd return home nearly dead, one mass of bruises and gore from head to foot, and 40 of his flock actually killed on the spot. I have known a plain, 16 miles broad, one sheet of water, to pass through which my horse often had to sink over his shoulder, and a little favourite dog had to swim frequently for an hundred yards. This may give some idea of our rains Ibid. þÿ

Ever, a tame goose shows much instinct and attachment : nod were its habits more clovly observed, the tame goose would be found to be by no means wanting in geneial cleverness. Its watchfulness at night time is, and has always been, proverbial; and it certain!) is endowed with a strong organ of sell preservation. Yon may drive over dug, cat, ben, or pig; but I dntv vnu to drive over a tame goose. As for wild geese, I know ol no animal, biped or quadruped, that is so difficult to deceive or approach Their senses ol hearing, seeing, and smelling are all extreme |y acute; independently of which, they appear to act in so organised and cautious a manner when feeding or roosting, as to defy nil danger. Many a time has my utmost caution been of no avail in attempting to approach these birds ; either a careless step on a piece of gravel, or an eddy of wind, however light, or letting them perceive the smallest portion of my person, has rendered useless whole hours of mancuovering. W ben a flock of geese has fixed on a field of newsow n grain to feed on, before alighting they make numerous circling flights round and round it, and the least suspicious object prevents their pitching. Supposing that all is right, and they do alight, the whole Hock lor a moment or two remains motionless, with crcot head and neck reconnoiioring the country round They then, at a given signal from one of the largest biids, disperse into

open order, and commence feeding in a tolerahlv regular line. FROM KINGSTON, J A MAIC A. fty the Backus, Capt. M alone y, we are in receipt of our files of Jamaica papers to the 7lh ultimo. The crop of sugar is coming in, and the article sells readily at rather higher prices than usual, in ftons"quence of the shortness of the crop. Sales for exportation are made at 22s tid to 28s 61, according to quality. þÿ Flour and Rice are in demand at improving prices þÿ half a cargo of Caroline sold at 22, þÿ while the other half was held at 24s. Holders of American produce were circulating reports that Mexico had declared war with this country, in order to advance the matlo't, but rio credit was given to the rumors, and the market remained flat. The population of Jamaica, in 1844, ac cording to the census, says the Despatch was 377,433. Of this number no less than 142,831 were returned as having no occupation ; that is to say, a number exceeding one tiiiid of the whole population of Jamaica were doing nothing. The Agricultural labourers were returned as 132.182, being 1 0.000 less than the number without occupation ; but from even that amount are to be deducted those who are agricultural laborers only bv name þÿ we labor on their own land, or, if they give occasional labor, to a sugar plantation, are driven to such exertion bv necessity Mr. Kubb. in his speech at F.xeter Hall, estimated those whose lab >r have been withdrawn, from regular estate's work, with their families, at 95 000 ; that is to say, he multiplied 19,000 fathers of families by 5,

the probable numbei of each family. At the period of the cessation of slavery, ii we remember rightlv : the slave population of this island was estimated at something like 300.000 soul-. Of these fully 200,000 were agricultural laborers þÿ in 1814 þÿ at the end of 10 years we find the laboring ngrieultniists of all denominations set down at 132 102, from whom are to be deducted Mr. liubb's 95,000, leaving about 40,000 to perform the entire woik ol the staple cultivation of the soil throughout the island. Any one who has acquaintance with the labor which is now obtainable on Sugar estates will bear us nut in stating that the average number of effective laborers to be met with throughout the island, does not exceed forty for each estate. We speak of the average, because some estates may have more, while many never see so large a gang. The Journal of yesterday estimated the numher of Sugar estates at t!l 1, so that of the above estimate there are not more than 25 000 laborers engaged in the cultivation of Sugar, out of a laboring population amounting, ten yeats ago, to 200,000. This is a condition of Society, continues the Despatch' " well deserving the attention of the British people. It is fraught with evils far beyond the mere injury to private interests which inust result from the impossibility of cultivating estates and producing sugars without labor It holds out a prospect of public calamity as the result of cmnncipa lion, which the most reckless will fear to contemplate. If the secession f«om profitable

Ihhor. that is to say, from that description of labor which enriches the nation as well as the individual, shall continue in the ratio in which it has receded since the abolition of slavery, another decade will find us without an estate in profitable cultivation. A Tame White Owl þÿ A friend of mine has sent me the following particulars respecting a tame wmie owl, which was taken, when young, fiom a nest in the woods at Diistone, near llexnam, in Northumberland, and given by a lady to her children, who brought it up. Great pains appear to have been taken to domesticate this owl, in consequence of which it became very familiar, in imitation ol us own call, it received the name ol keevie, to which it would leadily answer when wiiliin hearing, following the sound from whatever pari ol die premises it might happen to be in. Its usual place of repose during the day was under the branches of an old Scotch tir, which grew down a steep inac.ct ssible bank, where it would sit appa rently asleep, but sufficiently awake to en deavour to attract the notice ol any one who passed by its usual cry of kcevic, keevie þÿ One ol the most sinking peculiar ilies in this tame owl is said to have been iis fondness for music. Ii would often come into the drawing-room of an evening, on the shoulder ol one ol the childieu, and, on hearing the tones of the piano, would sit with its eyes graveiv fixed on ihe instrument, and ils head on one side hi an attitude of attention; when, suddenly spreading his wings, be would n 1 1 o t , t on the keys, and. milking a rlart at the pcrlormei's finger with bis beak, would continue hopping about, as if pleased with the execution. supper Irom the person who was in the habit ol loedin; him, and whom lie readilv permitled at such limes to lake him up, and carry linn into ihe house for this purpose. By andbye it was observed that lie did not devour his meal m the ki'chen as formerly, but fled along the passage dragging ihe meat alier him, till he reached the garden door, when he flew with it to a part of the shrubbery þÿ On being followed it was discovered that l:c had brought with him a companion, who not having courage to accompany him the whole way, remained at a respectful distance to receive his bounty. Alter having served bis visitor in this manner lie returned to the kitchen, and leisurely devoured his own portion. 1 his practice was continued lor some months, till at length one evening lie was missed, and nowhere to be found ; his companion, it is said, continued to visit the spot alone for several weeks uttering doleful cries, but could never be persuaded to come nearer to be fed. - , Fvcm Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, November 30, 1810 þÿFrance. The French papers are occupied with angry invectives against the thiee northern powers, for the annexation of Cracow. It is added, that some divisions have arisen in the Cabinet, the result ol which may lead to a partial change in the ministry, hut which will not affect the position of M. Guizot. This excellent minister continues to deserve, as well as to retain, the favour ot his master, and both together exhibit an example of firmness and moderation, which justly of entitle them to the reputation they possess, being the best minister and the most able Sovereign in Europe. Any dissensions in the Cabinet between M. Guizot and Ins coaib jutors seem to be as easily settled as in the case of disputes between the household and housekeeper in a þÿnobleman s family 1 he housekeeper is commanded to dismiss the refractor) servants, and to replace them with others which are more to her mind. 1 here is nothing in the trench Court like one or two contumacious members breaking up a cabinet; the King in such cases enters the council himself, and the matter is either amicablv settled on the spot, or M. Guizot receives an order to dismiss the oilemiiug members. The recent affair of Cracow, and the consequent necessity, or rather the occasion which it has afforded, of the closer union of the two kingdoms ol England and trance, has extinguished any angry fc< ling which might have been excited by the language of l.ord Palmerston in his recent correspondence. Nothing is now mentioned but the
expediency and sound policy of a nose union of England and France against the ambition and faithfulness of the northern powers.

Danger of Experiments with Gi n Cotton. þÿ þÿ Flic simple and inexpensive means bv which cotton may be converted into a dangerous explosive substance lias led many young men in this town to try experiments with it, in ignorance of some ol its peculiar and most perilous qualities; and we are therefore desirous to cautiou such persons against trying experiments with it until they are more familiar with its singular propeitics. The other day we noticed the bursting of a gun with a charge ol 83 grains of gun cotton, and we mention an experiment tried in this immediate neighbourhood the other day, showing that one fourth of this weight of the gun cotton is an ample charge for an ordinal y fowling piece. 20 grains of gun cotton (which is about equivalent in bulk to nn ordinary charge of gunpowder), in a gun of the usual construction and average bore, drove the ball at a distance of 50 yards through three boards each an inch in thickness, and also through a three inch plank þÿ these planks being reared up together þÿ and the ball was quite flattened against a L-rick wall about three inches behind the last plank. This shows the tremendous projectile force of the gun cotton, when properly prepared ; and the danger that must result from what, though a small quantity and weight of the cotton is still an over charge. Another peril should be mentioned as a caution to youth. The cotton does not need actual contact with flame, or even w ith a spark, to ignite it, but explodes on reaching a comparatively low

temperature, ns may be ascertained by placing a small quantity ton the warm hob ol a grate, out of the influence of the flames. In one instance an experimenter in this town þÿ held some of the prepared cotton in his hand before the lire, and it exploded and burned his hand. The same result attends the hold ing of a piece of the cotton at a considerable height above a gas light. It explodes when
held more than a vaid above the top of the flame It is said that it may even be spun into calico, and yet retain its explos ive power. þÿ Manchester duo ait a n .

The Prussian Universal Gazette publishes i he following ordonnanee, dated at Cracow : þÿ VVe, Ferdinand of Este, by the grace of God, Emperor of Austria, King of Bohemia and Hungary, &e. þÿ The peace of Vienna, of the 14th of October, 1809, had separated from our empire the city and territory of Ctacow, and annexed it to the grand duchy of Warsaw: but, subsequently to the events of the war of 1812, the Russian arms having reconquered them, our father, the late Emperor Francis, 1 , concluded with the allied Courts of þÿI russia and Russia, on the 2 1st of April, and 3d of May, 1815, a treaty, containing the following stipulation : þÿ Cracow, with its territory, will form in future a free and independent city, under the protection of the three powers. The express condition, and the necessary supposition of the arrangement. however, were, that the tiee city should observe the strictest þÿneutrality refuse all asylum to refugees, subjects of tfie three powers, þÿ ami deliver them into the hands of the competent authorities. A sad experience of ltl years lias demonstrated that Cracow has not fulfilled the conditions of its independent existence, and that since 1830 it has been the constant focus of intrigues against the three protecting powers. Finally, in the month of February of the present year, it became the theatre of more violent and dangerons scenes than ever. After the government and constitution had been overturned, and when t he fate of the city was abandoned to a handful

of conspirators, who had assumed the name of tiie Revolutionary Government of Poland, and excited to revolt against the existing authorities the inhabitants of all the ancient provinces of Poland, an armed horde invaded our dominions from the territory of Cracow, and it was necessary to replace it under a provisional government, subject to our military law, and to have it occupied by the troops of the protecting powers Those even's have precluded the possibility of restoring liberty and independence to Cracow, after their overthrow by the enemies of the order, repose, and tranquillity of Europe, and deeming it our duty to secure both our faithful subjects of Galicia and the peaceable inhabitants of Cracow against the attacks and intrigues of that anarchical party, we have, together with his Majesty the King of Prussia, and his Majesty the Emperor of Russia, taken into serious consideration the future fate of Cracow. þÿ With that view, deliberations have been entered into with the special plenipotentiaries of tire Courts of Berlin and St. Petersburgh, the result of which has been the conclusion of a convention, signed at Vienna, on the 6th of November of the present year, and in virtue of which l tie three protecting powers of t Ire city of Cracow revoke and suppress t he treaties of the 3d of May, 1815. That city and its territory consequently return under our sceptre, as they belonged, previous to the peace of Vienna of the 1 1th of October, 18t)9, to our late father and our ancestors. We

have, for that reason, taken possession of the city and its territory. We annex them for ever to our Crown, and declare them to form an inseparable portion id our empire, with which we incorporate them.

As the Piussian and Austiian commissioners, at the conference at Vienna, are said to have been authorised by their courts to arrange some commercial (natters interesting to the three powers, without being obliged previously to refer to Berlin and Petersburg, and as these relations do not appear to oiler any particular difficulties, it may be taken lor granted, that within a few days the publication of Ibis decision will take place in Gin cow, and you may therefore consider the abolition of the republic, and the te union ol this little territory with Austria, as already done. The continued existence of Cracow as an independent slate has been recognised as incompatible with the tranquillity of the Polish territory, and the safety ol Germany and the three powers, which without the cooperation and sympathy, nay, the slightest help of any other European power bad established the republic, as it were by way of trial, whether a shadow of Polish independence were still possible, resolved at length finally to abolish their own work, which bad

French Protection.-- Ah armament of 1,500 French soldiers, and a considerable supply of artillery, has just sailed from Brest for Tahiti, for the purpose of carrying the wrath and vengeance of Louis Phillippe and Mons. Guizot to the little band of patriots who have lately made such a noble stand on behalf of their island home against their gal lain protectors. The whole population of Tahiti is not above five or six thousand persons, women and children included, from which, il we deduct the aged and infirm the available fighting men cannot be equal in numbers to the augmented force of their invaders. The number of French soldiers already in the island is about one thousand, and as we have lately seen, those gallant gentlemen at arms have put forth their energies and burnt their powder more to their own damage than to that of the natives, whom they are determined, if possible, to destroy. It happens however, that the Tahitians understand much better than their enemies how to carry on the war in their mountain fastnesses. We are glad to find that already the London Missionary Society has memorialised the Government to the e licet we have stated, and is now calling upon its friends throughout the country to follow its example. The object of the proposed memorials is to entreat the Government þÿ first, « To adopt such measures, by negotiation or otherwise, as mav secure to the inhabitants of the Society Islands the peaceable and permanent possession of their country ; and,
secondly, to employ its friendly mediation with the Government of France to allow those natives who may be so disposed, peaceably to withdraw from the Island of þÿTahiti. þÿ Ibid.

In 1749 an advertisement appeared in the newspapers stating that on a certain evening a famous bottle conjuror would perform. He undertook to elicit the music of any known instrument from the walking cane of any of the audience, after which lie would walk into a quart bottle, placed upon a table in the middle of the stage, and sing in it. On the appointed night the house was crowded to suffocation, but, as the conjuror was tardy in making his appearance, fhe audience became impatient, and roared out for a return of their money. The stage-manager at last appeared ; exhorted them to keep quiet, and promised that their money should be returned if no performance took place. Some person in the pit called out that, if the ladies ard gentlemen who were impatient would pay double price, lie would walk into a pint bottle ! A burst of laughter followed the announcement ; the spectators became sensible tor the fust time, of their own folly, and a tremendous riot began. The discontented people of the pit and gallery tore up the benches, broke tire lamps, and made a complete wreck of the inside of the theatre. From Bell's Weekly Messenger, London, November 23, 1840 A GUAISO LOCALITY. The southern coasts of Africa are almost entirely destitute of harbours or shelter for shipping þÿ the only safe and commodious one is situated on the south west coast, in Int. 33, 8 south, and about 70 miles northwards from Gape Town. It is known as Saldariha Hay; but, until the last two years, it had been scarcely visited, except by voyagers who had occasion to make such repairs as require a vessel to be hove down. Last year some attention was called to this bay by the visit of a large number of vessels, for the purpose of obtaining the guano which abounded upon some of its islets; and since that period, about 40,000 tons have been removed from these barren shores, from north to south, the bay has an extent of about 25 miles, and its breadth mav be about seven. There are thiee small islands near its entrance bearing die names ot .luiteu, Malagas, and Marcus islands Between Jutten island and the main shore is a wide passage, deep enough for vessels of almost any buiden. Malagas island was coveied wi h guano seve nl feel in depth, and the captains of numerous vessels smit out to search lor die supposed nitrate of soda were glad to take home cargoes of guano. Many boatmen and labourers from Gape Town, as well as those brought bv the ships, and parlies of the crews, lived in tents upon this island for a considerable time, digging, drying, and carrying die guano, so thai quite a little town was formed. The bntcheis of ('ape Town sent men to slaughter the cattle

and sheep which the farmers of the interior drove down in large quantities as supplies for the ships. Shooting parties were often formed to chase the antelopes and baboons, which at one time abounded in die neighborhood, but soon retired belore the guns of the sportsmen. The baboons are about lour teet in height, and of tierce disposition, and, from their agilitv in scrambling among die locks, are not easily shot. The wnter was the spectator upon one occasion of a young baboon, which had been slightly wounded bv a musket ball, seizing a good sized dog, and ripping it open with bis poweiful teeth. There are also hares and rabbits, and oilier varieties of small game. Ostriches, loo, inhabit this sandy district, but, owing to their fleetness, seldom tall a prey to man, who is obliged to content himself with their eggs, which are found laid upon the sand to batch. One egg makes a good meal lor two persons, the contents being reckoned about equal to 25 Iipus' eggs. There are plenty of sea fowl þÿ penguins, duikers, shags, gnnnets. Asc. þÿ whose presence has rendered the soil ol the islets so valuable. There are also many varieties of noxious snakes, of which the cobra di cnpelln and the pull adder are the worst, Now that the vessels have lelt the place, it has reassumed its former s ilitarincss, and die game is reluming as before. On Marcus island eggs are laid in great quantities by duikers ami other sen birds. An old man who obtains a livelihood by collecting them, and sending them by the boat-

men to Gape Town, is the sole inhabitant. I he northern part of the hay is sepaialed Ironi the southern, which is called the lagoon or river, liy the two islands Schapen and Meenwon, which are also great egg licpasi

The lagoon extends about eight miles to the south cast, and at its extremity ate some tlats, where good salt may he obtained. To the east the rocks are chieliy granitic; in Hoetjes Bay there is a large quantity oi limestone, and masses of ironstone are frequently found. The bay contains a plentiful supply of good fish, very lew, however, resembling the European species; and thousands ot divers and other sea birds may be seen puisumg and diving for them A few years ago a lishery was set on loot, but it was ultimately given up lor want of sufficient market. A single stoic, at which most common articles may he obtained, a cottage or two close to the shore, and two or' thiee farm houses a lew miles inland, are all the habitations within ma n v miles ol this capacious bay. One ol these farms, about seven miles from lite sea, is called V V nit; Kuss, front a large while stone on ttie hill above it, which, owing to its elevated position, is a conspicuous object Iroin most parts ol the oiling, llete is a poweiful spring of water, verv slightly brackish. The ptopiielor is a Dutch boor, and owner of the land lor some miles along the north side of ttie hav lie cultivates scarcely anything, leav ing it in its natuial state, and allowing his cattle to feed on it. Most ol llic land aiound is a light sandy soil covered with

brush, with very little grass in summer, as there is not sufficient moisture in this dry climate. Willi respect to what has been the chief product of tins place þÿ ilie guano þÿ it lias generally been supposed to be the droppings ol sea birds accumulated in large quantities. This opinion may be correct as to that which comes from the coast of Peru, but it is not strictly so of African guano Both that which was procured at Saldanha Bay, and that at lchaboe, was largely mixed widi other substances. Some captains not inaptly coinpared it to " a mixture of bad snutl and rotten kittens" A few years since the seals and other marine animals along tins coast were seized with a fatal epidiinie, which caused them to crawl upon the rocks, and die in myriads. In this part rain seldom or ever lulls; and the dead bodies alter undergoing partial decompositon, became dried in the sun, and were overlaid by the deposits of the birds. This was the manner in which the guano was formed into beds of such depth, lu digging into it, the remains of fur seals were found in abundance. The preservation and accumulation of these animal deposits is caused by the climate, rain þÿ as in Egypt in a similar latitude north þÿ seldom falling to wash them awav. There is also a great similaiity between the climate of the African and Pel avian coasts in the w ant of rain ; arid ii has been conjectured, not without probn bililv, that there may he a field of guano enter pr se under liie same parallel of latitude
on 'lie Itllle explored coasts of A'ow Holland. þÿ Chamber's Journal.

IAVK IN MUX ICO Since the period when Herman Cortes Inst landed in A/exico, accompanied by 11 handful of desperate adventurers for the purpose of achieving the conquest of at) empire whose foundation reached beyond I tie annals of authentic history, whose people were numbeicd by millions, and where civilization had reached a point almost incredible to those who consider the present condition of that portion ol the new world, since thai epoch how great and how curious are the changes that have accrued. The fertile plains of Mexico, cultivated by a large arid industrious agricultural community, then yielded the fruits of the earth iu abundance, even to excess, feeding amply, not onlv the simple Indian husbandman, who tilled the ground, but even the luxurious noble þÿ for tbeie were nobles in the land, vvb 'se wide p e sessions equalled tlmse of our richest land nomas Now, it is with difficulty that the ilc- -I'd, nit of the caiiijuistndorps can procure a sallt t.citi a fium l.ls þÿlands su luvuuted by

In place ol the magnificent court of Montezuma, thronged with nobles in splendid costumes and the gaudily dressed followers composing the retinues tich 111 barbaric pearls and gold, there is the Court of a Santa Anna or a Paretics, with a scanty attendance ol soldieis and civilians clad in the sombie attire of modern Europe. For well otdered system of justice and police, we have lawless violence, and corrupted liibunuls; for a mild and good government, revolution and anarchy : for peace, a constant state of ferocious war, and lor prosperity þÿ can it tie wondered at from foregoing changes ? þÿ , dost.- poverty tution , and general misery.

The question that naturally suggests itself at this point is, what have been the causes ol this deplorable etiect. How can a period of scarce tlnee centuries have sufficed to produce such powerful changes. The tyranny of Gortes and his successors, bv destroying the independence, and breaking the spirit of the people, and bv greedily robbing them of their wealth, depriving them of all inducement to maintain their country in its former flourishing condition, may be the primary cause. The inordinate avarice and ambition of the governois sent out, at a later period by the mother country, who endeavoured, by every means of oppression and torture in their power, to squeeze from the natives the uttermost fraction they could contribute to swell the fortunes with which they hoped to return to Spain, helped still further to crush this unhappy country, And, lastly when the pcopie of Mexico, by throwing of the yoke of thraldom to a distant country, thought they would obtain a return of their former independence, and with it a return ol their former prosperity, the selfish plans of a few ambitious individuals frustrated their hopes, by their turbulence and intrigues. Since the revolt from Old Spain, Mexico has been the very hot bed of revolutions A few months has been the average duration of a Government, frequently a lev weeks. No merchant, 110 speculator, could think of embarking capital in such a country, no prudent person would think there of establishing himself. 'I lie morals of the people,

as may be concluded, are very lax, robbery and murder stalk about the streets at noonday, ail are tainted bv the looseness of manneis, from the highest to the lowest. The lady had just seated herself, al or having danced down 20 couple con spuito, to the tune of " Sir Roger de Goveriev," when a most alarming explosion took place arising it is supposed, from the ignition of the inflammable material by the extra heat communicated in the dance, or from the force with which the lady deposited her person on the bench.
